newsitem.title: GERMANY: MOTOR RACING-BENETTON ARE BACK IN THE FRAY.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-BENETTON ARE BACK IN THE FRAY.

text.p: Gerhard Berger's stirring German Grand Prix win for Benetton on Sunday suggests that the Formula One world title race may now be more than a private battle between Williams and Ferrari.

In fact Ferrari's Michael Schumacher could find the Italian team's former drivers constitute a stronger immediate challenge to his title ambitions than the Williams men, who both failed to finish at the German circuit.
The victory was Berger's first at Benetton since the Austrian joined the team from Ferrari last year.

He and French team mate Jean Alesi, also ex-Ferrari, are fourth and third in the overall standings respectively, behind Schumacher on 53 points and Williams' Jacques Villeneuve on 43. Alesi has 22 points while Berger has 20.
"It is looking a bit like we might be fighting with Benetton rather than Williams if they carry on the way they are," said Ferrari technical director Ross Brawn.
"I don't know why Williams were off the pace this weekend. It's very surprising but I think it is a minor aberration rather than a trend for the rest of the year."
However Brawn said Williams did need to make a big improvement in performance to prevent Schumacher securing his third world title and the Italian team's first since 1979.
Brawn, who masterminded Schumacher's two previous championship successes with Benetton in 1994 and 1995, said the German was now full of confidence.
"He is very confident and, if we can make sure the car is reliable, it will take a lot to stop him," explained Brawn.
"If we can get the car to the finish line then there is a very good chance of the championship. The performance of our car is adequate to give him a chance."

Williams lost further ground on Sunday after Germany's Heinz-Harald Frentzen failed to finish the first lap after colliding with Ferrari's Eddie Irvine and Villeneuve spun out of the race on the 34th lap.
Benetton, with their first victory since 1995, had Brawn suggesting that they, and not Williams, could be Ferrari's main challenger over the rest of the season.
"I don't know why this weekend went so badly for Williams but if practice is not right then things deteriorate.
"Villeneuve had to start too far back and Frentzen was in fifth instead of on the front row. It was a bonus for us as you would normally expect Williams to be on the front two rows," he said.
Williams have scored just 39 points since the San Marino Grand Prix in April, while Schumacher alone has won 42 during that period.
Having started the season as clear favourites, the British team has had its advantage trimmed away as rivals, particularly Ferrari, made great strides in development.
The team's technical director Patrick Head refused to comment at length about their hopes although he did say that he believed Williams could still beat Schumacher.
Williams' problems will almost certainly be compounded if Benetton do stage a revival during the rest of the season.
Berger, who claimed the 10th win of his career at Hockenheim, believes they can regularly challenge for podium positions from now on.
"I believe we are going to be competitive until the end of the season," explained the 37-year-old.
"There is no reason to believe we are ahead, although I think we are competitive and we have a good chance to compete for points and podium places at the end of the season."
The British Jordan team could upset the form-book too. Italian Giancarlo Fisichella led the race and was set for second place when he had a puncture with six laps to go.
The Benetton-bound driver was confident the team would score their first victory since entering the sport in 1991.
"The car was really quick at Hockenheim, it was good in testing at Monza and we could have finished on the podium in Germany," he said.

"The next race is in Hungary, which is very tight and twisty, but it is more or less like Monaco and I qualified fourth on the grid there. I am very confident that Jordan can win a race this season." REUTER
